extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; reformers, policymakers, and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria for judging and selecting forms of government, focusing on which institutions best promote present good government and improvement of citizens' faculties. Emphasizes the superiority of representative systems and the civic effects of different regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt government to the people's stage of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of government best for a people is the one which 'tends most to give them that for want of which they can not advance, or advance only in a lame and lopsided manner.' Leading-strings (temporary tutelage) may be admissible only to train people to 'walk alone.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the immediate impediments to progress and choose the polity that supplies what the people lack without destroying what they already possess. Beware of institutions that carry a people to one stage but permanently incapacitate them for the next (examples: Egyptian hierarchy, paternal despotism of China).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government as the ideally best form
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill's proposition: 'this ideally best form of government will be found in some one or other variety of the Representative System.' The ideally best form is that which, given necessary conditions, would favor and promote all forms and degrees of improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an ideal of the most eligible government (in itself) and then test practicability against the people's conditions; where practicable, the representative system is preferred because of its combined present and prospective benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereignty vested in the entire aggregate; citizen participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideally best form 'is that in which the sovereignty, or supreme controlling power in the last resort, is vested in the entire aggregate of the community, every citizen not only having a voice... but being, at least occasionally, called on to take an actual part in the government by the personal discharge of some public function.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether citizens have real opportunities and duties to participate personally in government (local or general), not merely passive or symbolic roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights secure only if individuals can stand up for them
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights and interests of any person 'are only secure from being disregarded when the person interested is himself able, and habitually disposed to stand up for them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether institutional arrangements enable individuals to defend their own rights (representation, voice, access to forums), since exclusion increases risk of overlooking or sacrificing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosperity proportional to personal energies enlisted
rubrics_metrics.description: General prosperity 'attains a greater height, and is more widely diffused, in proportion to the amount and variety of the personal energies enlisted in promoting it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare regimes by how well they enlist a wide range of citizens' energies (economic, intellectual, civic) in public life; freer systems that mobilize more participants tend to produce higher and broader prosperity (historical comparisons: Greek cities, Italian republics, England vs despotic states).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of absolute power impedes civic and moral development
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms concentrating power (even a 'good despot') lead to a people 'without any potential voice in their own destiny' — their intellectual, practical, and moral faculties are stunted because they exercise no public will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge regimes for their long-term effects on citizens' capacities: does the system encourage thinking, public spiritedness, and initiative, or does it produce passivity, bureaucracy, and narrowed sentiments?

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should not produce servility; it must foster desire for freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Any education 'which aims at making human beings other than machines, in the long run makes them claim to have the control of their own actions.' Education that strengthens faculties will create appetite for freedom rather than passive obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess state education and civic formation on whether they cultivate citizen autonomy and the desire for participation, rather than training subjects to be submissive instruments of rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary dictatorship permitted only to restore freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption of absolute power as a temporary dictatorship 'can only be excused... if the dictator employs the whole power he assumes in removing the obstacles which debar the nation from the enjoyment of freedom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exceptional concentrated power only as a strictly limited, transitional measure whose explicit aim and practice are to re-establish conditions for popular government; otherwise it risks entrenching despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusiveness: extend participation impartially to all
rubrics_metrics.description: Though benefits of freedom have historically 'been obtained by the extension of its privileges to a part only of the community,' 'a government in which they are extended impartially to all is a desideratum still unrealized.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate representation and franchise by inclusiveness: exclusion leaves interests unguarded and reduces incentives for self-improvement among the excluded; full participation is the ideal to strive for where practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should promote active character over passive
rubrics_metrics.description: Political institutions should favor the 'active' type of character (which struggles against evils and strives to make circumstances bend to itself) rather than the 'passive' type (which endures); 'improvement in human affairs is wholly the work of the uncontented characters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a regime cultivates enterprise, public spiritedness, and dispositions to improve collective life, because active citizens drive intellectual, practical, and moral advancement while passivity fosters envy and stagnation.
